posts.content_md:
I know we touched breifly on this a while ago and Jeff B. informed me of the only necessary chemicals needed in the fix bath for DCG. As I purchased these a while ago, I thought it would be nice to open the discussion back up and get to it in the lab.

Here is what I have so far.

I plan to mix 2 grams of Aluminum Sulfate per 150ml water to be used as a hardener.

I plan to mix 2 grams of Sodium Metabisulfite per 150ml water to be used as the Dichromate reducer.

Alkali removes the hardening (of Kodak fixer or Aluminum Sulfate), make DCG less sensitive and increases storage time.

Acid increases hardening, make the DCG more sesitive and decreases storage time.

Alum decreases swell of gelatin through bonding but if emulsion is too swollen, no or less crosslinking is achieved. 

Swelling is mimimized at 4.5 ph.

6.5ph good starting poing with nice swelling with addequate hardening and good sensitivity.

Now, separating these processes makes me think. 

First I believe I will soak the plate in sodium metabisulfite to get rid of the unexposed Dichromate. I am not sure if I can adjust the ph of this bath but I know I can adjust temperature to change the swelling amount.

Then place the plate in the Aluminum Sulfate to harden the unexposed regions. Now since the unexposed regions have been swollen (the exposed regions do not swell due to heavy crosslinking), the croslinking in the unexposed regions will be much more spread out due to point number 3 above. This is what makes the "honeycomb" latice support network in the unexposed regions in which the water in between this latice network will be ultimately replace by air.

Then process in alcohol and dry.

I am really excited about trying these two chemical independently! I think I am really starting to understand the mechanics of what happens to the amino strand (gelatin) from cooking to drying. Of couse all of the above is only a starting point and concentrations, temps, ph, which bath to use first, etc will need to be worked out.

Any feedback before this weekend is appreciated.

Jeff, if you please, I believe I can lower the ph of the Alum by adding a little sodium metabisulfite, but can i use some sodium carbonate to raise it? Or will either of these take away from the reducing action of the alum or cause some other adverse effect? Toxic fumes are not welcome.... 

John.

posts.topic_title: Alum and Sodium Meta instead of Kodak Fixer
posts.author: jeff-blyth
posts.post_subject: Alum and Sodium Meta instead of Kodak Fixer
posts.content_md:
John , you asked:

"..................Jeff, if you please, I believe I can lower the ph of the Alum by adding a little sodium metabisulfite, but can i use some sodium carbonate to raise it? Or will either of these take away from the reducing action of the alum or cause some other adverse effect? Toxic fumes are not welcome.... "

Sodium metabisulfite is a combination of sodium sulfite and the unpleasant

acidic gas sulfur dioxide(SO2). So you can smell SO2 a bit in solutions of 

sodium metabisulfite which are automatically acid as you imply, so adding sodium carbonate will raise pH and take it back towards being sodium sulfite which in neutral or alkaline solution is not smelly. Sodium sulfite is a less active reducing agent than the metbisulfite, but even so it is a rapid 

reactor with dichromate. 

Aluminum Sulfate

A problem with Alum is that you cannot get its pH up to neutral level

with sodium carbonate without an aluminum carbonate precipitate forming so

you may have to settle for no higher than pH 5. But As a matter of interest What is the pH of your Kodak fix solution you normally have used please? 

Jeff

posts.topic_title: Alum and Sodium Meta instead of Kodak Fixer
posts.author: JohnFP
posts.post_subject: Alum and Sodium Meta instead of Kodak Fixer
posts.content_md:
First, remember that it was Jeff Blyth that stated SM and Alum could be used instead of Fixer. I am not sure if his original suggestion stated using them separate or not, but I love the idea of having another control (variable lol) in the process.

Well, I have been told in the past that understanding how the DCG process works for a layman like me is nonsense and will not help make a better hologram. While this might be true, I will have to say I do have an understanding. Though correct or not, it is what I believe thus far with the information I have gathered.

The one eye opener for me is I realize when we process an exposed DCG hologram we are not really processing the exposed areas but the unexposed areas.

When I use hardening in the following, it is the same as stating crosslinking and vise versa. 

I will try to explain what I believe is going on and apply it to this system.

When collagen is broken down a lot of bonds between the amino chains is broken but not all. This dictates the harness and other properties of the gelatin. Then when we make an emulsion of DCG and coat a plate. At the exact time we coat the plate most bonds between the Amino chains that are not the permenant ones left over from the gelatin creation process from collagen are broken. Th.ese were weak bonds. As the gelatin dries and matures a dark reaction occures. This dark reaction is a hardening process which we will call Ha1. This hardening happens throughout the entire emulsion. We then expose the emulsion to light, or more specifically interference fringes. In the light struck fringes there is additional hardening which will will call Ha2, much more so then in the non light struck fringes. We can then allow an additional dark reaction time, which I believe happens more quickly in the exposed regions then the unexposed regions which we will call Ha3.

Then with this process the hologram is placed in the reducing agent (SM). This reduces the CrVI to CrIII throughout the plate and thus no more hardening in the emulsion. At this point the SM solution does expand the emulsion. In the light struck areas we have a weak Ha1, a strong Ha2 and a strong Ha3 as compared to the non light struck fringes which have a weak Ha1, minimal Ha2 (except for the continued dark reaction in that dark fringe) and a weak Ha3 (again only dark reaction occuring). So the expansion dictated by the relative hardnesses of the fringes is much more in the unexposed areas then in the exposed areas. So since the expansion is mainly in the unexposed area, we will look at this area only. I envision that most crosslinking has already happened that is possible in the ideal hologram in the light struck areas. But in the non light stuck area the cosslinking is minimal which allows greater absobtion of water. The temperature of this SM bath is the most important property at this point. The hotter the SM the larger the expansion. The lower the temp the less expansion. I also believe that there are amino strands in the unexposed areas that are not crosslinked at all and these get washed out. In other words there is a loss of gelatin in the unexposed regions. Temperature also plays a role in this too. The higher the temperature the more gelatin is lost in this area.

It is then we place the plate in the Alum. To have full control of the expansion desired, I would make the temperature of the Alum the same as the SM. Now the Alum is also a hardener but how it crosslinks I am not sure. I think it has to do with PH. But the crosslinking can only occure if the amino chains are within a certain distance of one another. They have to be close. So the Alum crosslinking is not complete in the unexposed regions. I believe it is this that allows the support of the exposed fringes and keeps the unexposed regions from collapsing thus letting the exposed regions fall onto one another. So, the hotter the SM and Alum then less hardening and the cooler the SM and Alum the more hardening in the unexposed region only. But too hot and hardly no crosslking and we get a collapse. Too cool and to much crosslinking and we lose our differential between exposed and unexposed regions

Find that balance in between with just the right temperature and we get just the right amount of crosslinking to provide enough support to keep the exposed fringes from collapsing on one another but enough open non crossliked spots to allow us to ultimately replace the water therein with air, giving us out greatest differential of index of refraction.

Back to answering you question, now that you know what theory I base my answer on, I believe that when the emulsion is swollen, again mostly the unexposed regions, and the Alum is done just right the unexposed regions shrink back to their original thickness once the water is taken out. The reason we dont get a wavelength shift is the amino chains are like springs. When we stretch in the water we do two things. One is we separate some such that their cannot be a hardening from the ALUM and secondly we harden lightly the amino chains that are close enough.

So how can we red shift? I proposed taking the final hologram and placing it in a solution of AmDi and water and exposing it to light. I believe this is still true but now I see there may not be enough amino chains close together to get that freezing of the expansion I wanted. 

Now I wonder, is a small amount of gelatin disolved in the AmDi and water would not be much better. That is, take a final hologram that we want to red shift and place it in a 100:3:3 (Water:Gelatin:AmDi) and then expose it to light. The gelatin amount will need to be tested as too much will fill in too much of the voids in the unexposed regions and too little will not achive the shifted needed.

I hope this makes sense, and anyone can feel free to comment or correct anthing. Or even add their opinions unless of couse no one want to go out on the thin lonley limb with me for fear of being wrong.

John, take another look at the paper by Blyth, Lowe, Pecora, Improving the remarkable photosensitivity of dichromated gelatin for hologram recording in green laser light: 

> One of us (JFP), after much experience in producing very bright holograms by the conventional method, was quite surprised to discover only recently that leaving out the fixer had a far more detrimental effect than leaving out the hardener (alum).(...) we can form the reasonable assumption that the holographic exposure initially produces in the light-struck fringes a transformation of Cr(VI) to a Cr(V) form which must be necessarily bound to the gelatin matrix – otherwise the moment it was immersed in water it would migrate away and the future integrity of the fringe structure as defined by the future formation of Cr(III) crosslinks would be gone. Meanwhile the dark fringes must still contain chromium which is still virtually all in the Cr(VI) state and once immersed in water this chromium is free to migrate away. Now here perhaps lies the key point. We conjecture that unless that Cr(VI) does manage to leave its sites within the dark fringe it could be reduced there by the strong reducing agent bisulfite/sulfite and become indistinguishable from the Cr(III) in the neighbouring light fringes. So the fringe contrast would be lost (except for the relatively small amount of oxidized gelatin exclusively in the light fringes).So, to now maximize the fringe differences in the wet step using the Kodak Fix, what is required is for the light induced and immobilized Cr(V) species to be much more quickly reduced by the sulfite ions than the unbound Cr(VI) species in the adjacent dark fringes. We can assume hthat this situation is helped by the probability that any Cr(V) intermediate produced in the dark fringe would not be bound to the gelatin as it is not produced by the oxidation of the gelatin but by the oxidation of suflfite ion. This would mean that until the Cr(VI) in the dark fringe is reduced down to Cr(III) it will not bind to the gelatin.

posts.topic_title: Alum and Sodium Meta instead of Kodak Fixer
posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.post_subject: Alum and Sodium Meta instead of Kodak Fixer
posts.content_md:
> **Dutchelm05:** During post exposure, there is a time when the DCG film is left in the dark for 5-10 minutes. What is that doing?

Exactly what happens is a pretty speculative question, I'd say. But I'll throw in my two cents worth.

I look at exposure as a way of speeding-up the normal dark-reaction. DCG has the normal tendency to get harder as time passes. Exposing it with light accelerates the hardening effect in those areas. An oddity of DCG is that, once the light is removed, those areas that previously "saw the light" remain pretty excited and stay that way for a long time.

In that excited state, the hardening rate is faster, compared to areas that did not see the light. The dark areas are also getting harder, but at a much slower rate (i.e., the "normal" dark-reaction).

The excited areas gradually get less and less excited as time passes (after the light has been removed). They are most excited immediately after exposure, then, ever so slowly, they get less and less excited. Seconds after the light is removed, the rate of hardening in the exposed areas FAR outstrips the normal dark-reaction hardening of the unexposed areas. So most of the benefits gained by leaving the DCG in the dark after exposure occur in (say) the first 5 minutes, then continually get weaker over the next hours, then even weaker over the next days, and still weaker over the next weeks. So after a month, the exposed areas may still be getting harder at a faster rate compared to the unexposed areas. But the difference may be quite small, perhaps negligible. Leaving it alone for the first 5 or 10 minutes is probably the most helpful from a practical standpoint, but I have a paper that says the longer, the better. They were even getting better diffraction efficiency after leaving them alone for a month before processing them.

posts.content_md:
> **Dutchelm05:** Thank you for the answer. It is starting to gel (no pun)Can you elaborate on dark reaction? What is it exactly? Is it to do the the unexposed region? Or when I am out in the sun too long?Many thanksTony

A good question ! ----- It needs a chemist to do it justice because it is complicated.

Although it straightforwardly means it reacts slowly with gelatin without light being involved as Joe suggests it does need some explaining. If you are not interested in the finer chemistry detail then stop reading here .

Most oxidizing agents such as oxygen in the air, nitrates (saltpetre as in gunpowder etc) , and chlorates can be mixed with combustible materials and just sit there inactive virtually forever unless something such as a lighted match gives them that vital spark which triggers the chain reaction and rapid burn up. So these oxidants need what’s called “activation energy” as a kick start. However in the case of dichromates the chromium is a member of what is known in the Periodic Table as “transition metals” . These are inclined to have the peculiar ability to indulge in low activity with little activation energy which is why they are used universally as catalysts for low temperature reactions. They have variable valency which is why we have referred in this forum to CrVI going to Cr V going to Crlll The transition metal iron in our blood is doing this sort of low temperature oxidation work for us of course too. The transition metal effect is to do with atomic orbitals where the electrons have a large array of complicated empty orbitals to whizz about in some of the time and sort of get through barriers without having to be kicked to jump over the normal activation energy barrier that non- transition metal ions have to do. 

A non- transition metal such as say Aluminum which is always Al 111 in

 our water based alum chemistry here and cannot be reduced or oxidized to a different valency but it does make complexes with the gelatin and hardens it (but not quite as strongly as Cr111). 

So back to dichromate which has 6 electrons missing from its uncombined metallic state. The electrons have been taken mainly by 3 oxygen atoms in a not very stable arrangement and these electrons are actively whizzing around the Cr atom’s empty orbitals as well as their main base around the oxygen atoms. Energy is gained for the system if they can return permanently to the Cr atom by being instrumental in getting the oxygens to swap them over by taking other electrons in organic groups in the gelatin to

give more stable arrangements producing partially oxidized gelatin.

So the dark reaction of dichromate is primarily a matter of oxidation of the gelatin without a kick start with light energy or extra heat and it can be slowed down in a ‘fridge but needs to be in a freezer to really slow it down. 

Incidentally the less pure the dichromate the more it contains other transition

metals such as copper and the more it enables this catalysed oxidizing effect to occur in the dark. More acidity also increases it which is why the more acidic ammonium salt in unexposed gelatin film gives it a shorter shelf life than the potassium salt.

So, my guess that ammonia vapour is alkaline was correct.

That now raises the next question: After blow drying the ammonia out of the gelatin, would it help to hyper sensitize the plate in another container that contains a sponge that has been soaked with acetic acid?

Perhaps this brings the balance of the dichromate<=>chromate even more to the left and makes the colour more orange and thus more likely to absorb our green laser light.

So perhaps this procedure for G307:

- Mix 10ml of 4% Dichromate with .1ml of clycerin and a drop of fotoflow.

- Put a drop of this solution on a gelatinated plate and spread the drop evenly with a piece of plastic (just like with diffusion method).

- Discard the remaining Dichromate solution.

- Let the plate dry vertically.

- Store the plate in a stock container that contains a sponge that has been soaked with ammonia.

- When ready to use a plate, take one out of the stock container.

- Blow dry the plate.

- Place the plate some time in the re-activation box (a container with a sponge that was soaked with concentrated acetic acid).

- Expose the plate.

- Develop the plate (heat or SM)

Actually I think intuition is the right thing to use provided you have the basic rules straight then you will be more likely to sense the end result correctly even if the actual mechanism is fuzzy .

For example you have not got the rules quite straight about dichromates and chromates so your intuition is handicapped.

Chromate salt is not free of the dark reaction that Tony asked about above. That "transition metal" effect is still there chugging away very slowly but formulations with alkaline chromate will last for weeks at room temperature whereas dichromate formulations will only last for days at room temperature.

In any case there is no sharp pH point where dichromate is fully turned into chromate , it is gradual transition as you go up the scale. So at pH 

9 say there is still some dichromate and if you remove it then more chromate will break down to replace it because it is in equilibrium at that pH. To understand this more, first we need to consider the importance that Chromic acid has as it comes into this chromate/dichromate business as follows.

Chromic acid (made from chromium trioxide and water: CrO3 + H20 ----> H2CrO4 *note it now has 2 H's replaceable by a metal ion or ammonium ion*) 

It reacts with bases such as potassium hydroxide to give the potassium chromate salt :

H2CrO4 + 2KOH -----> K2 CrO4. 

This chromate salt has the ability to combine loosely with another molecule of the acid to make dichromate salt like this apparently:-

K2CrO4 + H2CrO4 ------> K2Cr2O7 + H2O where the formula for dichromate is what you get when you evaporate the water off but

in water it is in reality K2CrO4.H2CrO4 so it has 2 acid hydrogens and it is an acid salt although the straight formula on the bottle K2Cr2O7 does not look like an acid with replaceable hydrogens. 

However I think I am going to win $10 from you from my intuition because I know that 

Potassium chromate in water is a slightly alkaline salt (typical pH reading is about 8. ) whereas potassium acetate is a slightly more alkaline salt

pH reading close to 9. So what this means is that acetic acid is **weaker** than Chromic acid . ie. the stronger the acid the more the pH of its potassium or sodium salts tend to be neutral. So HCl gives neutral KCl and very weak carbonic acid gives alkaline potassium carbonate and ultimately

taking water (H-OH)itself as an acid it gives the ferociously caustic KOH. (I once left a saturated solution of KOH in a glass bottle and after about a year it had managed to eat its way right through the glass!)

So I think I might win the $10 because I believe that Chromic acid is significantly more acid than acetic. (It has a lower "pKa" value where

[Ka = (H + X )/ HX and X is (COO-) for acetic or CrO4 for chromate.] where "p" means the negative log as in pH). 

In simpler terms acetic acid is not strong enough acid to turn potassium chromate (K2 CrO4) into dichromate (K2Cr2O7). (However HCl vapor will do it, but then you get bad secondary problems---- the dichromate proceeds to oxidize the HCl to chlorine gas---Ugh! )

So if you carry out your good idea of de-activating potassium dichromate with ammonia gas then you will *in effect*get the 2 salts potassium chromate and ammonium chromate being formed although strictly speaking you would technically get a double salt like this:

K2Cr2O7 + NH4OH (ammonium hydroxide from NH3gas plus H2O) ---------> 2K(NH4)CrO4 (which is no different in effect from half a molecule of each of K2CrO4 + (NH4)2 CrO4.)

Here endeth the Chemistry lesson.--Amen

Jeff

Great experiments John,

Perhaps there is some competition between swelling and hardening taking place in the plate after all:

**- Plate submerged in Alum only:** Alum hardens the plate all over, but washes some of the Cr(V) out of the emulsion before it can be hardened by the SM. => weak fringe structure and milkiness. 

**- Plate submerged in SM only:** SM hardens the fringes, but at the same time there is some uneven swelling because of the water penetrating and swelling the gelatin at the same time. => random fringe spacing and more milkiness.

**- Plate submerged in mix of SM+Alum:** Alum very quickly hardens the plate throughout a little bit, allowing the original fringe structure to be preserved when the SM hardens the fringes.
